label: 4r
quote: Im Gegensatz zu meiner bisherigen Auffassung scheint es, ist gerade das Gleich ($=$) eine Negation, nämlich die von Verschieden ($\neq$).
english: Contrary to my previous view, it seems that it is precisely equality (=) that is a negation, namely that of 'different' (≠).
topic: Philosophical notes on mathematics as the foundation of natural laws, the Lorentz transformation as an example of pre-established harmony, axiomatics as a 'super-consciousness', and the idea that equality (=) is the negation of difference (≠).

triage.modern_statement: This is a conceptual question in foundations, not a precise conjecture. It asks which relation should be taken as primitive: equality (=) or difference (≠). In modern terms: should 'different' be the basic positive notion, with x = y defined as ¬(x ≠ y), rather than defining ≠ as ¬(x = y)? In constructive mathematics this is the theory of apartness. One takes a primitive positive inequality relation # (irreflexive, symmetric, cotransitive) and defines equality as its negation, x = y :⇔ ¬(x # y). When this negation coincides with equality, the apartness is called 'tight'.
triage.answered_by: The idea was developed by L.E.J. Brouwer and A. Heyting, though the sources found do not connect it to Hilbert's note. Brouwer introduced the apartness relation in his intuitionist work around 1919–1920s as a positive form of inequality on the continuum. Heyting later axiomatized apartness and used it in axiomatic geometry and algebra (late 1920s). Taking apartness as primitive and defining equality as 'not apart' is now standard in constructive mathematics (Bishop-style analysis, constructive algebra, formal proof systems such as Coq). I found no source showing that Hilbert's note influenced, or responded to, Brouwer's work.

evidence.claim: Brouwer introduced the apartness relation as a positive analogue of inequality on the continuum. Heyting later introduced apartness axiomatically to treat axiomatic geometry and algebra.
Brouwer's idea was that equality might not be a primitive concept and could be defined as the negation of a strong notion of inequality called apartness.
In constructive mathematics, apartness is a constructive form of inequality and is often taken to be more basic than equality.
The negation of an apartness relation is an equivalence relation. The claim that every equivalence relation is the negation of some apartness relation is equivalent to excluded middle.
Brouwer used negation to define new relations between mathematical objects, starting from the constructively defined relations of coincidence and apartness between points of the plane.
Apartness is still in current use in constructive algebra and formalization: work on constructive fields with apartness, and generalizations to 'difference relations'.

triage.why: Hilbert's remark is a philosophical observation, not a problem with a definite solution. It is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. Its content is the same as a concept that was later worked out in detail: intuitionistic/constructive apartness (Brouwer, then Heyting), where equality is defined as the negation of a primitive positive inequality. That theory is standard and still studied (constructive algebra and analysis, proof assistants, difference relations). Confidence is medium for three reasons: the page is undated here, I found no source linking this note to Brouwer or Heyting, and 'solved' fits only in the sense that the idea was later developed systematically, not that a specific conjecture was proved.
